rationale: A wins because it knows where the evidence line is: "Half a million secondhand Patagonia items later, the company still won't say if resale pays" is a real disclosure story and the proof list demands the missing denominator. B keeps bluffing with "something no major apparel brand has attempted" and "designed to shorten its own sales pipeline," neither of which exists in the update. A has one bad overreach, but it flags holes before they become embarrassing pitch copy.
gaps_in_A: "A company with no shareholders" overstates the supplied fact. The update says Patagonia is privately held and directs profits to environmental causes, not that it has no shareholders.
"nobody else can copy the math" and "publicly traded peer who can't do this" are too absolute without competitor economics or repair-cost data.
It misses a possible customer-experience/service angle. "Not for consumer lifestyle desks" throws away a viable story if Patagonia can produce a real repair example, turnaround time, and price list.
gaps_in_B: "something no major apparel brand has attempted" is invented. No competitor benchmark appears in the update.
"designed to shorten its own sales pipeline" turns a hypothesis into fact. The update does not say repairs reduce new-item purchases or that Patagonia designed the program for that purpose.
"no publicly traded apparel company could defend to shareholders" is boardroom fan fiction unless an analyst, executive, or cost comparison backs it.
"journalist-fit-check" is the wrong next step. This set needs proof and newsworthiness triage first because two main angles are built on unsupported premises.
